title: What replaces anchors and pinning once sessions restore panes?
body:
decade has two kinds of pane (`Kind` in `src/panes.rs`). An anchor waits for a window with a given app id and stays as an empty slot when its client exits. A transient pane is removed when its client exits. The pin on the bar turns one into the other.

Persistent sessions change what a pane needs to remember. herdr's panes are slots that hold a process and know their cwd. On restore it starts a shell there, and resumes agents with their own resume command. If decade restores panes the same way, an app-id rule may be the wrong thing for a pane to hold, and pinning may mean "keep this pane across restarts" rather than "wait for this app id". decade-7c65be, a pinned terminal that never gets its client back, sits on the same question.

Jack decided on 2026-11-07 that this deserves its own discussion before anything changes.

## Open

- What a pane holds: an app-id rule, a command and cwd, or both.
- Whether pinning survives, and what it means once every pane is saved.
- Whether the three starting anchors (chat, terminal, code) stay special or become an ordinary default layout.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/575e4e76
notes.text: Part of this is settled by the workspace design in decade-4c2624: the chat, terminal and code anchors stop being the default, and --chat and --code are removed. What a pane holds and what pinning means are still open.
